title: API Design
description: Design APIs that are intuitive, version-safe, and performant. Compare REST, GraphQL, and gRPC, and learn versioning, idempotency, rate limiting, and error handling conventions.

data.text: APIs are the contracts between services. A good API is easy to use, hard to misuse, and stable enough that clients do not break when you change the backend. A bad API creates hidden coupling that slows down every team that depends on it.
As a senior engineer, you will choose the right API style for each use case, design consistent conventions, and evolve APIs over time without disrupting clients.

REST, GraphQL, and gRPC each solve different problems. REST is simple and widely understood. GraphQL lets clients request exactly the data they need. gRPC is fast and strongly typed, ideal for internal service-to-service communication.

cards.title: REST
cards.description: Resource-oriented architecture using standard HTTP methods and status codes.
cons: Over-fetching or under-fetching data is common
Multiple endpoints needed for complex queries

cards.title: GraphQL
cards.description: Query language where clients specify exactly the fields they need in a single request.
cons: Caching is more complex than REST

cards.title: gRPC
cards.description: High-performance RPC framework using Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2.
cons: Less human-readable than REST or GraphQL
Limited browser support without a proxy

data.text: APIs change. Versioning is how you manage change without breaking existing clients. The three main strategies are URL versioning, header versioning, and content negotiation. Choose one and use it consistently across all your APIs.

data.title: Versioning Approaches
items: Header versioning: Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2 — cleaner URLs but harder to test
Content negotiation: Same URL, different request body schemas — most flexible but most complex

data.text: An idempotent API produces the same result whether you call it once or many times. POST is typically not idempotent — calling it twice might create two orders. PUT and DELETE are usually idempotent. For non-idempotent operations, use idempotency keys.

data.title: Idempotency Key Example
data.content: A payment API accepts an Idempotency-Key header. If the client retries after a timeout, the server recognizes the key and returns the original response instead of charging twice.

data.text: Rate limiting protects your system from abuse and ensures fair usage. Return standard HTTP status codes: 429 Too Many Requests when the client exceeds the limit. For errors, use a consistent response format so clients can parse and react programmatically.

data.title: Industry Standard
data.text: Stripe's API error format is widely admired for its clarity. Include an error type, a human-readable message, a unique request ID for support, and a link to documentation. Clients should never need to parse raw stack traces.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Choose REST for simple public APIs, GraphQL for flexible client queries, and gRPC for internal high-performance communication
Version APIs from day one using a consistent strategy
Make writes idempotent using idempotency keys
Return structured error responses with request IDs for debugging
Rate limit all public APIs and return 429 with Retry-After headers
data.takeaway: APIs are long-lived contracts. Design them carefully because changing them later is expensive.

items.question: When should I use GraphQL over REST?
items.answer: Use GraphQL when clients have diverse data needs that would require many REST endpoints. Use REST when your API is simple, widely cached, and consumed by external third parties.

items.question: How long should I support old API versions?
items.answer: Support each major version for at least 12 to 18 months. Announce deprecation timelines clearly and give clients migration guides with code examples.

items.question: Should API contracts be managed centrally?
items.answer: Yes. Use OpenAPI for REST, GraphQL schema files for GraphQL, and .proto files for gRPC. Store contracts in version control and review changes like code.

data.title: Design an Orders API
data.description: Design a versioned REST API for creating, retrieving, and updating orders. Include endpoints, request/response schemas, error codes, idempotency handling, and rate-limit headers. Write the OpenAPI description for at least three endpoints.
data.expectedOutcome: An OpenAPI 3.0 document covering POST /orders, GET /orders/{id}, and PUT /orders/{id}, with error schemas and idempotency key support.
